title: Pardoned by Trump and escaping charges at home, ex-Honduran leader’s case shows a nation’s struggle for sovereignty
text:
Share article

Print article

A Honduran judge on Sept. 1, 2026, dismissed a sprawling money-laundering and fraud case against the country’s former president, Juan Orlando Hernández. It was the latest stroke of good fortune for Hernández.

Hernández returned home in late July after an eventful four years outside Honduras. He was extradited to the United States in 2022 following a multiyear, nonpartisan U.S. investigation. In 2024 he was convicted of cocaine trafficking and related charges and sentenced to 45 years behind bars in the U.S. Yet after serving only 18 months of his sentence, Hernández was pardoned by President Donald Trump.

Hernández remains a forceful power broker behind the scenes of the current Honduran government, led by President Nasry Asfura of the right-wing National Party.

Yet as a scholar of Latin American politics, I believe Hernández’s return to Honduras, and his successes evading legal accountability, are emblematic of something broader than impunity for elites: His case demonstrates the struggle for sovereignty in a country facing a renewed form of U.S. intervention.

Hernández’s return to Honduras on July 26 was symbolic. He landed at Palmerola International Airport, which shares its runway with the Soto Cano Air Base, a longtime staging ground of U.S. interventions in Honduras.

While Hernández was greeted by National Party supporters, for many Hondurans his pardon and return to the country were seen to undermine hopes for justice and adversely affect the political process.

When Trump first announced plans to pardon Hernández, it was on the eve of the Honduran elections in November 2025. In another sign of meddling from Washington, Trump endorsed Asfura and threatened to cut off aid to Honduras if Asfura, who was trailing in opinion polls leading up to the elections, did not win.

On Dec. 1, the day after the election and with Asfura and center-right politician Salvador Nasralla locked in a technical tie as vote counting continued, Trump issued a full pardon for Hernández. U.S. officials then hurried to provide special immigration protections for Hernández, and a specialized tactical team drove him from a West Virginia prison to the luxury Waldorf Astoria hotel in Manhattan.

Back in Honduras, the pardon was seen as a “green light for the National Party to manipulate the vote,” as a former high-ranking U.S. diplomat told ProPublica. Trump’s actions signaled that Washington supported the National Party’s engagement in electoral manipulation, as election observers and academic experts say happened in 2017 with Hernández’s unconstitutional second presidential term election.

Following weeks of suspicious delays and fraud allegations, Asfura was announced the winner on Dec. 24, 2025, by a margin of less than 1 percent.

Although free from the U.S. justice system, Hernández still potentially faced charges in Honduras.

On Dec. 9 the Honduran attorney general reactivated an international arrest warrant for Hernández over charges of fraud and money laundering.

These charges are part of the corruption case known as Pandora, a scheme that embezzled $12 million in public funding and allegedly diverted that money into political campaigns, including Hernández’s 2013 presidential campaign.

Previous Pandora trials accused major National Party figures, yet during Hernández’s presidency a special appeals court dismissed the cases. But under the left-leaning administration of Xiomara Castro – from 2022 to 2026 – Honduras in 2023 indicted former National Party presidents Hernández and his predecessor, Porfirio Lobo.

Hernández remained in the U.S. until his international arrest warrant was suspended, returning to Honduras shortly before his initial trial. On Aug. 12, 2026, the Public Ministry confirmed the charges against Hernández and presented 48 pieces of evidence. Yet after two weeks, the court dropped the charges against Hernández.

With the National Party back in power, few believed Hernández could be held accountable in Honduras, particularly given that the Honduran judicial system is plagued by targeted violence that undermines the rule of law.

Indeed, impunity is virtually guaranteed for the wealthy and powerful. And that is something Hernández helped ensure.

Under his presidency, Honduras passed legal reforms specifically reducing sentences for money laundering and protecting politicians from investigations for embezzlement. Foreshadowing the likely outcome of Hernández’s trial, Lobo was acquitted days before Hernández’s return.

Although Hernández’s trial is over, controversy over his return remains. That’s in part because of explosive new allegations that surfaced in May 2026.

The Spanish media outlet Canal Red released 37 audio messages allegedly with the voices of politicians, including Asfura and Hernández. According to the leaked audio files, a scandal known as HondurasGate, Hernández’s return was merely one part of an international scheme to undermine left-wing Latin American governments and expand foreign militarization in Honduras.

Those implicated dismiss the files as AI-generated propaganda. While independent analysis suggests the files are likely authentic, valid suspicions from independent sources have emerged casting doubt on their veracity.

Regardless of the HondurasGate audios’ authenticity, much of what they outline echoes wider concerns over external pressures reshaping the region’s politics and expanding militarization.

Trump has been open about seeking to secure right-wing allies throughout the Americas. Weeks after pardoning Hernández’s narco-trafficking, the Trump administration raided Venezuela to arrest President Nicolás Maduro on alleged narco-trafficking charges.

Meanwhile, the U.S. continues to use sanctions in Cuba in an aggressive push for regime change on the island, and has used varying degrees of influence to try to affect elections in places from Colombia to Brazil.

In Honduras, the National Party – and especially Hernández – has been a willing partner in tying its own national priorities to those of the U.S. and close U.S. allies, including Israel.

Hernández cultivated strategic importance as an ally of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Trump. Israel and the U.S. have long provided military technology and security aid to Honduras, and both are expanding military involvement there.

Recently, Honduras signed a memorandum expanding defense cooperation with Israel, and U.S. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth announced agreements for joint military operations on Honduran, Colombian and Guatemalan soil, similar to ones in Ecuador.

The motivation behind Trump’s support for Asfura’s election and Hernández’s return is also related to advancing controversial charter zones in Honduras known as ZEDEs, the Spanish acronym for Zones for Employment and Economic Development.

Trump allies in Silicon Valley, including Peter Thiel of PayPal and Palantir, are leading investors in Próspera, one of the ZEDEs.

Passed in 2013 under Hernández, the ZEDEs are a highly contested sociopolitical experiement; they create spaces of privatized governance within Honduras that essentially forfeit Honduran sovereignty to U.S. tech titans seeking havens from government regulations and oversight.

The ZEDEs were deemed unconstitutional under the Castro administration, leading Próspera’s billionaire investors to sue Honduras for nearly $11 billion. Now, with the National Party back in power, a renewed corporate push is underway and the ZEDEs are moving forward rapidly, including in Afro-Indigenous territories.

Ultimately, Hernández’s case shows the extent to which a right-wing vision is currently winning in Honduras and, from critics’ standpoint, the risks that vision poses to democratic governance and sovereignty.

As foreign corporations and billionaires secure access to Honduran resources, average Hondurans are struggling. There have been massive politicized layoffs in the public sector. Doctors in the public health system report going months without pay since President Asfura, who also named himself secretary of health, entered office. Meanwhile, private healthcare and agribusiness have received multimillion-dollar government contracts.

At the same time, ongoing U.S. immigration crackdowns are hurting the Honduran economy, which is heavily dependent on remittances. While Hernández remained in the U.S. until he was safe to return to Honduras, the same is not true for thousands of Hondurans who are being deported, often despite fears of violence.

Yet while ordinary Hondurans face rising insecurity, including increasing homicides and disappearances, a special unit of Honduran forces was designated to protect Hernández.

That’s the privileged political environment Hernández spent his career building – and from which he again directly benefits back in Honduras.

Associate Professor of Political Science, University of Nevada, Reno
